questions.question: Eve intercepts a message encrypted with a Caesar shift using an unknown key k. What is her most efficient attack?
options: Count letter frequencies across thousands of messages
Try all 26 possible shifts and keep the one that reads as English
Wait for a known-plaintext weather report
questions.explanation: A Caesar shift has only 26 keys, so brute force is instant. The other attacks work but are overkill here.

questions.question: In RSA, why must e be chosen with gcd(e, (p−1)(q−1)) = 1?
options: So that the ciphertext is smaller than the message
So that e has an inverse d modulo (p−1)(q−1)
questions.explanation: A number has a multiplicative inverse modulo k exactly when it is coprime to k. Without an inverse there is no decryption exponent d.

questions.question: The RSA correctness proof shows m^(ed) ≡ m mod p and mod q separately. Why is that enough to conclude m^(ed) ≡ m mod n?
options: Because p and q are distinct primes, so if both divide m^(ed) − m then pq does too
Because n is always larger than m
Because Fermat's Little Theorem works for any modulus
Because e and d are both odd
questions.explanation: Two different primes dividing the same number means their product divides it. Fermat's theorem alone only covers prime moduli, which is why we split n.

questions.question: You know x ≡ 2 (mod 3) and x ≡ 3 (mod 7), with 0 ≤ x < 21. What is x?
questions.explanation: Numbers ≡ 3 mod 7 below 21 are 3, 10, 17. Only 17 leaves remainder 2 mod 3. CRT promises this answer is unique mod 21.
